extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents, and patent examiners dealing with PCT filings and national phase entry in India
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural / substantive standards for international (PCT) applications and entry into the Indian national phase, and for substantive examination and grant of patents in India. Covers fees, transmittals, withdrawals, international search/preliminary examination, national phase requirements and patentability criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of formal defects; consequence of non-correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Deficiencies such as lack of a title of the invention, lack of an abstract, or physical defects must be corrected within prescribed time limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such defects are not corrected within the prescribed time limit the Application is considered withdrawn. All actions regarding non-compliance are subject to PCT Receiving Office Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmittal of record, search and home copies; timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office transmits the 'record copy' of the International Application to the International Bureau and the 'search copy' to the International Searching Authority, while keeping a third 'home copy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transmittals do not take place while national security prescriptions apply. The Office mails the record copy promptly and in any case not later than five days prior to the expiration of the 13th month from the priority date. The search copy is transmitted at the time of transmittal of the record copy except where the search fee has not been paid on time; in that case, search copy transmittal occurs after the fee is paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT fees and correction of underpayment
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT fees are subject to change; applicants must refer to the latest PCT newsletter for current fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transmittal fee as per schedule. Failure to pay or underpayment can be corrected under PCT Rule 16bis — Receiving Office will issue an invitation to pay missing fees. Payment may be made within one month from international filing date or later with a late payment fee. Specific payment instructions (e.g., Indian applicants remit certain fees in US Dollar by Demand Draft to SBI New York Branch) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and availability of International Search Report (ISR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Search Report is established by the International Searching Authority designated in the international application and has typical availability timings depending on priority claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no priority is claimed, ISR normally available within nine months from international filing date; if priority is claimed, usually by the 16th month from priority date. ISR is normally available before publication, allowing applicant time to withdraw before publication if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 19 amendments after ISR
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may amend the claims under Article 19 in light of the ISR, with effect in all designated States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time limit for Article 19 amendments is two months from transmittal of ISR to the IB and applicant, or 16 months from priority date, whichever expires later. Amendments received by the IB after the applicable time limit may, in certain circumstances, be considered received on the last day if they reach the IB before technical preparations for publication are completed. Such amendments save costs of filing different sets of amendments in designated Offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of Indian Patent Office as ISA/IPEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian Patent Office has been recognised as an International Searching Authority and an International Preliminary Examining Authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the IPO begins operations as ISA and IPEA, international search and examination reports for international applications filed in the Patent Office will be issued by the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of international application (Rule 90bis.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may withdraw the international application at any time prior to expiration of 30 months from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal is effective on receipt of a notice addressed by applicant, at his option, to the International Bureau, the receiving Office or, where Article 39(1) applies, to the IPEA. No international publication occurs if the notice reaches the IB before technical preparations for publication are completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of designations (Rule 90bis.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may withdraw designation of any designated State at any time prior to expiration of 30 months from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal of the designation of a State which has been elected entails withdrawal of the corresponding election. Withdrawal of designations of all designated States is treated as withdrawal of the international application. No international publication of the designation occurs if withdrawal notice reaches IB before technical publication preparations are completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of priority claims (Rule 90bis.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may withdraw a priority claim made under Article 8(1) at any time prior to expiration of 30 months from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If withdrawal changes the priority date, subsequent time limits computed from the original priority date shall be computed from the resulting priority date, subject to exceptions. The IB may proceed with publication on the basis of the original priority date if notice reaches IB after technical preparations for publication are completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of supplementary search request (Rule 90bis.3bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may withdraw a supplementary search request at any time prior to transmittal to the applicant and IB of the supplementary international search report or declaration that no such report will be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal is effective on receipt of a notice addressed to the Authority specified for supplementary search or to the IB, provided the notice reaches in time to prevent the transmittal. If not, the report or declaration may still be communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of the demand or of elections (Rule 90bis.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may withdraw the demand or any or all elections at any time prior to expiration of 30 months from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal is effective upon receipt of a notice addressed by the applicant to the International Bureau. If submitted to the IPEA, the IPEA marks date of receipt and transmits it promptly to the IB; that date is treated as date submitted to IB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for withdrawal notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices of withdrawal must, subject to exceptions, be signed by the applicant or, if multiple applicants, by all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant considered common representative under Rule 90.2(b) is not entitled to sign on behalf of others. If an inventor-applicant required by a designated State cannot be found after diligent effort, a notice need not be signed by that applicant if it is signed by at least one applicant and a satisfactory statement explaining the lack of signature is furnished, or if certain rule-specific signature requirements were complied with (e.g., Rule 4.15(b) or Rule 53.8(b) as applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences when an application, designation, priority claim, supplementary search, demand or election is withdrawn under Rule 90bis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal has no effect in any designated or elected Office where processing or examination has already started under Article 23(2) or Article 40(2). Where international application is withdrawn, international processing is discontinued. Withdrawal of supplementary search request discontinues that supplementary search. Withdrawal of demand or all elections discontinues processing by the IPEA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of International Preliminary Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: International Preliminary Examination is optional and provides a second opinion on patentability criteria prior to national phase expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It helps applicant adapt the international application according to ISR results; if the report is negative, abandoning can save national-phase expenses. Opinions from ISA & IPEA are non-binding on member countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent International Preliminary Examining Authorities (for Indian applicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of IPEAs competent for Indian applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Austrian Patent Office (AT), Australian Patent Office (AU), European Patent Office (EP) (only if ISA was AT, EP or SE), China IPO (CN), United States PTO (US), Swedish Patent Office (SE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand requirements for International Preliminary Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for international preliminary examination must be filed separately and meet formal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand may be made to IPO, IB or any competent IPEA; must contain prescribed particulars, language and form, and payment of prescribed fees within prescribed time limit. Demand must be made within 22 months from priority date or within 3 months from transmittal of ISR and written opinion or declaration under Article 17(2), whichever is later. Fees are given in PCT Newsletter.

rubrics_metrics.name: General national phase timing (PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The national phase follows the international phase and requires filing a national phase application in each designated country within prescribed PCT time limits (at least 30 months from priority date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Member countries may increase this time limit by national law. India provides 31 months from priority date with no scope of extension. Some countries allow extension on payment of additional fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic requirements to enter national phase in India
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements and formalities to enter the Indian national phase from a PCT international application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT national phase application is a convention application under Section 135; file within 31 months from priority date or international application date (whichever earlier). Pay prescribed national fees and file a duly verified translation of the basic application if not filed/published in Hindi or English. The title, description, drawings, abstract and claims as filed with the international application are taken as the complete specification; at time of national phase filing no other amendment shall be allowed to the complete specification as filed in the international application. Amendments made before ISA/IPEA may be taken as amendments before the Patent Office if applicant so desires. Change in applicant name after international filing may be effected by filing Form 6 and/or Form 13. If PCT/IB/304 (priority document) is available on WIPO website, IPO will not require submission; if not available, Office may request it. If applicant fails to comply with priority document requirement after invitation, priority claim may be disregarded. All other formalities required for ordinary patent application apply. Processing of national phase application will not commence before expiry of 31 months, unless applicant files an express request in Form 18 for early processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for examination (Form 18) and time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: An application will not be examined unless applicant or another interested person files a request for examination in Form 18 with prescribed fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request must be filed within forty-eight months from the date of priority or date of filing, whichever is earlier. If not filed within time limit, application is treated as withdrawn. Where a secrecy direction under Section 35 exists, request may be made within six months from revocation of secrecy or within forty-eight months, whichever is later. The Office will not examine an application unless it is published and a request for examination has been filed. If request is filed by an interested person other than applicant, examination report is sent to the applicant only; intimation given to the interested person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference for examination; examiner assignment and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Once request for examination is received and application published, application is taken up for examination in chronological order of filing of requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent application is referred to an Examiner by the Controller for formal and substantive examination according to the subject matter and examiner's area of specialization. Currently IPO has four examination groups: (a) Chemistry & allied, (b) Biotechnology/Microbiology & allied, (c) Electrical/Electronics & related, (d) Mechanical & other subjects. Reference to the Examiner is made ordinarily within one month from date of publication or one month from date of request, whichever is later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report of Examiner — scope of examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner makes a report to the Controller after detailed examination regarding patentability under Section 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report is prepared after conducting a prior art search to ascertain novelty, and examining whether the invention is inventive and industrially applicable. Examiner also checks whether invention falls under categories of non-patentable subject matter (Sections 3 and 4) and whether there are other lawful grounds of objection to grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search by the Examiner — databases and recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners conduct searches across national and international patent and non-patent literature and must record details of the search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Databases include Indian Patent Database, EPO, WIPO, USPTO, JPO, TKDL, and PCT minimum required databases (STN, QPAT, QWEB, DELPHION) and non-patent literature including technical/scientific journals. Examiner records: international classification; search strategy adopted; keywords used; language of search; databases consulted; list of search statements; final findings; limitations on search (e.g., unclear claims, multiplicity); and analysis indicating similarities with citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (what constitutes new / anticipatory disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is new if it is not anticipated by prior publication, prior use or prior public knowledge; prior art means everything disclosed to the public before priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indian patent applications filed before the date of priority but published after may be prior art. Prior art is anticipatory if all essential features of the invention are present in the cited prior art. Prior art should teach the invention explicitly. Relevant date for novelty is the date of priority. Mosaicing of prior art documents is not followed in determination of novelty. Generic disclosure does not take away novelty of a specific disclosure (e.g., 'metal spring' does not take away 'copper spring'); conversely, a specific disclosure takes away novelty of a generic disclosure (e.g., 'copper spring' takes away 'metal spring').

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step — general principle and person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step involves a technical advancement or economic significance that makes the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the art; invention must involve one or more inventive steps to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner first checks novelty then whether claimed invention involves inventive step. 'Person skilled in the art' is a notional skilled practitioner aware of general common knowledge at the relevant date and with routine means and capacity for work/experimentation; such person would have access to documents cited in search report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of inventive step — analysis approach
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventive step determination, examiner relies on all or any prior art revealed during search to decide if prior art teaches the claimed invention; invention considered as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications existing on priority date are considered. It is insufficient to deem a claim obvious just because individual parts are known separately — the claim must be assessed as a whole. Mere verification of previous predictions without substantial technical/economic advancement means lack of inventive step. For establishing obviousness, citing a mosaic of prior arts is permissible provided such prior art is enabling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability (usefulness) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be capable of industrial application — capable of being made or used in an industry — to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner shall assess if claimed invention is capable of use in any industry or made using an industrial process. Typically industrial applicability is self-evident; if not, mere suggestion is insufficient. A specific utility should be indicated in the specification supported by the disclosure. For example, indicating a compound may be useful in treating 'unspecified disorders' or having 'useful biological' properties is insufficient — specific usefulness must be specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable subject matter — frivolous inventions / contrary to natural laws (Section 3(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention which is frivolous or claims anything obviously contrary to well-established laws (e.g., perpetual motion) is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: machine purporting to produce perpetual motion; machine alleged to give output without input; machine claiming 100% efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable subject matter — contrary to public order or morality (Section 3(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention whose primary or intended use or commercial exploitation would be contrary to public order or morality, or cause serious prejudice to human, animal or plant life/health or to the environment, is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: devices/methods for theft/burglary, counterfeiting currency, gambling; inventions causing serious prejudice to life/health/environment (e.g., adulteration of food); methods likely to violate social/legal norms (e.g., human cloning); terminator gene technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable subject matter — discovery vs invention (Section 3(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere discovery of a scientific principle, abstract theory, living thing or a naturally occurring substance is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difference between discovery (discloses something already existing) and invention (creates a new product/process involving technical advance). A discovery that leads to a practical application (e.g., a process or article) may be patentable; a scientific theory alone is not. Finding a new property of a known material is a discovery and not patentable by itself, but an article or process using that discovery may be patentable if novelty and inventive step are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable subject matter — mere new form of known substance lacking enhanced efficacy (Section 3(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of known efficacy, or mere discovery of new property or new use of known substance, or mere use of known process/machine unless resulting in a new product or employing a new reactant, is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation clarifies that salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations and other derivatives of known substance are considered the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy. Examiner applies test case-by-case; complete specification should clearly and categorically show how subject matter differs significantly in efficacy. Case law (Novartis AG v. Union of India) interpreted 'efficacy' as 'therapeutic efficacy' for pharmaceutical substances — applicant expected to show comparative details demonstrating enhanced therapeutic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable subject matter — mere admixture vs synergistic combination (Section 3(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A substance obtained by mere admixture resulting only in aggregation of properties of components or a process producing such substance is not patentable; admixtures showing synergistic properties may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synergistic effect should be clearly brought out in the description by way of comparison at filing. Subsequent submissions of synergy data may be accepted in reply to office action as further support but such submitted data is not allowed to become part of the specification. Examples: soap, detergent, lubricant, polymer compositions may be considered patentable if synergistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentable subject matter — mere arrangement, juxtaposition or duplication (Section 3(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere arrangement/re-arrangement or duplication/juxtaposition of known devices each functioning independently in a known way is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be patentable, an improvement or combination of known matters must be more than a mere workshop improvement and must independently satisfy inventive step; the combination should produce a new result or a better/cheaper article. A 'combination invention' requires functional reciprocity or a combinative effect beyond sum of individual effects; mere collocation where each element functions independently is not patentable (examples: umbrella with fan, bucket with torch, clock and transistor in single cabinet). However, when old integers are combined with working interrelation producing new/improved result, patentability may arise.
